strengths: Novel multi-level non-IID problem formulation with clear taxonomy of hierarchical data structures in federated learning
Technically sound methodology with intuitive three-level decomposition (global, cluster, personalized) and additive aggregation scheme
Includes convergence analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) with detailed proofs, providing theoretical grounding
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple non-IID settings with numerous strong baselines (FedAvg, FedProx, FeSEM, FedRep, Ditto, etc.)
Adaptive structure discovery mechanism automatically determines number of levels and cluster structure without prior knowledge
Addresses practical concerns with communication efficiency analysis and multiple practical techniques (progressive level adding, model pruning)
Well-organized presentation with clear problem motivation and good use of visualization (Figure 1 taxonomy)
weaknesses: Convergence rate bounds not clearly characterized in standard O(·) notation, making theoretical contribution incremental and comparison with other FL methods difficult
Empirical improvements are modest and inconsistent - many results show <1% gains, questioning practical significance given added complexity

Experimental evaluation limited to synthetic image classification tasks (Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100) with artificial non-IID partitions; lacks evaluation on real-world heterogeneous data or other domains
Key design choices lack principled justification: model pruning threshold fixed at ε=0 with no sensitivity analysis, level adding rule appears ad-hoc, clustering algorithm selection not compared
Important limitations (increased storage/computation costs, privacy concerns with multiple models, fairness implications) relegated to appendix instead of main text discussion
Limited scalability analysis - only 50 clients tested; unclear how method scales to realistic federated settings with thousands of clients
Theoretical novelty appears incremental, combining existing ideas (additive modeling, clustering FL, personalization) without fundamental new insights into multi-level learning
Lack of clarity on practical implementation details: model discovery mechanism at intermediate levels, initialization sensitivity, convergence criteria for progressive level adding
Figure 4 suggests FéMAM discovers similar structures for multi-level [3,8,11] and IID settings, questioning whether hierarchical structure captures true heterogeneity or overfits
Code availability claim unclear - abstract mentions availability but provides no link, hindering reproducibility verification

strengths: Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figures 1-2 effectively convey the hierarchical structure)
Addresses a practically relevant problem: heterogeneous non-IID federated learning with hierarchical client structures
Comprehensive convergence proofs provided with detailed appendices
Consistent empirical improvements over multiple baselines on designed hierarchical non-IID settings (1-3% gains)
Communication efficiency competitive with standard FL methods
Progressive level-adding algorithm is a reasonable design choice for adaptive model complexity
Tests method across multiple non-IID data partitioning strategies
weaknesses: Catastrophic failure on IID data: 32.70% accuracy vs. FedAvg's 59.98% on Tiny ImageNet—this disqualifies the method as a general-purpose FL approach and raises reliability concerns
Limited novelty: straightforward combination of three well-established concepts (FedAvg + clustered FL + personalized FL) without sufficient new insights or techniques

Vague algorithm specifications undermine reproducibility: 'sufficiently small validation loss' undefined (Algorithm 1), pruning threshold ε set to 0 (no-op in practice), hyperparameters t and L not justified

Convergence analysis incomplete: explicit convergence rate never stated; key assumptions (D.1-D.5) only in appendix; Assumption D.2 on mapping function compactness is restrictive and practically questionable
Unjustified design choices: additive modeling combination not motivated (why not weighted ensembles or learned combinations?); regularization term λ/2∑||θ^(l) - Θ_{C(i)}||² appears ad-hoc
Artificial problem setup: multi-level hierarchy is pre-defined by data partitioning strategy, not discovered by the method; sensitivity to hierarchy misspecification not analyzed
Modest empirical gains: 1-3% improvements without statistical significance testing; gains do not justify added complexity and hyperparameter tuning burden
Limited experimental scope: only two vision datasets (Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100), only small ResNet-9 model, no modern architectures (ViT, BERT) or non-vision domains
Incomplete ablation studies: unclear contribution of global vs. cluster vs. personalized components; no sensitivity analysis for L, K, or data partition choices
Reproducibility concerns: how practitioners would construct multi-level hierarchies for arbitrary datasets is unclear; no guidance on choosing λ, ε, t, L parameters
IID performance explanation insufficient: Appendix A's 'No Free Lunch' justification is unsatisfying for a federated learning method that should work across heterogeneity levels
Storage overhead not thoroughly analyzed: each client stores L models; scalability to large models (BERT, GPT-scale) not addressed
Missing recent baselines: some hierarchical/multi-level FL and recent personalized FL methods not compared

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: First to formally study multi-level hierarchical non-IID structures in federated learning, addressing a practical gap in the literature where real systems often have implicit structure at multiple granularities

Elegant technical solution: The multi-level additive modeling framework that jointly learns global, cluster, and personalized models is intuitive, interpretable, and technically sound with clear mathematical formulation
Solid convergence analysis: Provides rigorous theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1-2) with clearly stated reasonable assumptions, supporting the proposed approach

Comprehensive and well-designed experiments: Multiple datasets and non-IID settings, extensive baselines from global/clustered/personalized FL, thorough ablations, and excellent visualizations of learned structures (Figures 4, C.1-C.2)
Thoughtful algorithmic design: Practical components like progressive level adding, model pruning, and efficient training with subset of levels show careful engineering for real deployment
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over competitive baselines across different non-IID scenarios, with particularly strong performance on cluster-wise and multi-level partitions
Reproducibility: Code availability, detailed hyperparameter settings (Appendix C.1), clear experimental procedures, and multi-run results with error bars
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Convergence analysis largely adapts existing federated learning techniques to the multi-level setting rather than introducing fundamentally new mathematical tools or insights

Unclear practical utility of structure: Ablation study (Table 2) shows excluding certain levels often has minimal performance impact (<2-3%), raising questions about necessity of complex multi-level hierarchy in practice
Limited experimental scope: Only evaluated on two image classification datasets (Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100); applicability to other domains, tasks, or modalities unclear

Insufficient practical guidance for hyperparameter selection: How to choose number of levels L and cluster numbers K_l in new applications without ground truth structure is not clearly addressed; validation-based discovery may not reliably detect true structure

Incomplete cost analysis: Communication overhead and storage requirements for maintaining multiple models per client not thoroughly analyzed in main paper; communication efficiency relegated to appendix
Limited discussion of structure mismatch: How the method performs when true data distribution doesn't match the assumed hierarchical structure not explicitly addressed
Incomplete sensitivity analysis: Method has many hyperparameters; limited exploration of sensitivity to model pruning threshold ε, clustering algorithm choice (K-means), and number of levels L

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing unknown multi-level heterogeneity in federated learning without requiring pre-specification of hierarchy depth or cluster counts
Practical adaptive framework with dynamic grow-and-prune mechanism that achieves communication efficiency (one model per round) while enabling multi-level personalization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple non-IID settings (cluster-wise, client-wise, multi-level) with consistent empirical improvements and detailed structure visualization
Consistent outperformance of diverse baselines from three paradigms (global, clustered, personalized FL) across simulated and foundation model experiments
Careful theoretical analysis with convergence bounds and monotone descent property across levels
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: additive modeling, multi-level structures, and boosting-style training are from prior work; contribution is primarily combining existing ideas rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques

Critical assumption (D.5 on boosting edge/residual alignment) is never empirically validated; lacks justification for when level-l outputs align with residuals in non-convex neural network optimization
Convergence analysis provides only asymptotic bounds without finite-time rates or explicit sample complexity; theory-practice gap regarding pruning dynamics not formally addressed
Experimental scale insufficient for federated learning standards: only 50-71 clients versus realistic deployments with thousands/millions; limited to image classification and text generation tasks
Fixed hierarchy configuration (L=5, K=[1,5,5,50]) across all settings despite claiming flexibility; unclear whether 5 levels necessary when most clients accept only 2-3 levels after pruning
Validation set used for both pruning (Eq. 7) and checkpoint selection creating overfitting risk; no analysis of validation data requirements or robustness to noisy signals
Missing key ablations isolating contributions of each component: pruning impact, multi-level vs. deep personalization, and per-level improvement breakdown not provided
Theory assumes level-by-level training with frozen lower levels but does not formally analyze grow-and-prune dynamics in Algorithm 1; validation-based pruning criterion lacks formal justification

strengths: Well-motivated multi-level non-IID perspective with clear intuition (Fig. 1)
Comprehensive experimental breadth across multiple datasets and non-IID settings
Practical level-wise training strategy that is communication-efficient and enables adaptive stopping
Adaptive hierarchical structure discovery via client-specific pruning avoids fixed architectures
Consistent empirical improvements shown across different evaluation scenarios
weaknesses: Limited novelty: framework primarily chains existing techniques (FedAvg + K-means clustering + local fine-tuning). Multi-level FL and additive modeling are well-established; the main contribution is routine extension to L levels with pruning

Critical unfair experimental comparisons: FeMAM maintains up to 50 personal models (Table 2) while baselines like FedEM use only 5 total. No capacity-matched comparisons provided. Claim of being 'cost-friendly' contradicted by inference overhead (Table 4: 4.7 models vs baselines with 2)

Weak theoretical contributions: Appendix D provides only standard averaged-gradient convergence analysis. Critical Assumption D.5 (residual alignment) is unjustified—no mechanism in Eq. (6) ensures boosting-edge alignment. Constants (γl, Bl, εl) are uncharacterized and problem-dependent

Severely limited experimental scale inappropriate for federated learning claims: 50 clients in simulations and 71 clients in foundation model experiments. Real FL systems operate at 1000+ scale. Multi-level structure [3,6,11] is artificially constructed, not discovered from real data

Incomplete ablations: no isolation of contributions from (i) multi-level structure, (ii) additive composition, (iii) pruning, (iv) boosting training. No comparison with simple two-level alternatives or capacity-matched baselines. Statistical significance of improvements unclear (e.g., Table 1 Cluster-wise differences overlap in standard deviations)

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: L=5 chosen empirically (Fig. 6), K=5 deemed 'insensitive' based on limited range [2-25]. No methodology for practitioners to set these in new problems. Pruning criterion (Eq. 7) is simplistic and requires validation data (not always realistic in FL)

Unjustified design choices: no justification for additive composition over alternatives (weighted averaging, gating). Residual learning analogy to He et al. (2016) is loose—models train independently, unlike skip connections within unified architectures

Suspicious implementation details: code availability listed but not provided ('Code:' placeholder), recent citation dates (2025, 2026) in a 2026 submission, instantiation highly specific (Table 2) despite claims of generality

Missing comparisons with cited baselines: Guo et al. (2024), Zhang et al. (2024), Li et al. (2025a) are mentioned but not experimentally compared. No analysis of failure modes or when multi-level hierarchy is harmful

Oversold motivation: claims about 'increasingly complex non-IID patterns' lack empirical evidence. Fig. 1 illustrative but not grounded in measurements of real systems. Multi-level structure is a modeling assumption, not a validated discovery

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing realistic multi-level heterogeneity in federated systems; compelling smartphone example demonstrates practical relevance
Elegant and flexible technical framework: additive composition across levels can instantiate different FL strategies without architectural constraints; genuinely generalizes prior 2-level approaches

Cost-efficient design: communicates only one model per level per round (same per-round communication as single-model FL) while enabling progressive multi-level personalization; adaptive inference via structure pruning

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: three diverse non-IID settings, 9 strong baselines, consistent improvements across all settings including foundation models (Table 1), detailed ablations (L, K sensitivity), and insightful convergence analysis (Fig. 4-5)

Solid theoretical contribution: convergence analysis correctly decomposes within-level (standard averaged-gradient) and across-level (boosting-style) convergence; monotone non-increasing objective sequence (Eq. D.18)
Clear presentation: well-written with effective visuals; algorithms clearly specified; comprehensive appendices with experimental details and convergence proofs
weaknesses: Somewhat incremental contribution: combines established techniques (additive modeling, clustering, personalization, boosting growth) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts; the innovation lies in integration rather than novelty of components

Assumption D.5 (residual alignment) lacks empirical validation: crucial for boosting improvement guarantee (Eq. D.16-D.17) but never verified experimentally; failure modes when assumption is violated are not discussed, weakening confidence in theoretical guarantees

Limited experimental scale: only 50 clients in simulated setting and 71 in foundation model experiments—far below realistic deployments; authors acknowledge (Section 6) that real scenarios involve 'harder, more diverse tasks' but don't evaluate at that scale

Client-side validation-based pruning (Eq. 7) may be problematic: no discussion of sensitivity to validation set size, data imbalance, or how heterogeneous clients with limited validation data make pruning decisions; could lead to incorrect structure for data-sparse clients

Modest improvements in some settings: CIFAR-100 Cluster-wise shows 53.72% vs. 53.29% (FedCAM)—marginal gain; Tiny ImageNet Client-wise shows 60.46% vs. 59.11%—improvements don't always justify added complexity

Limited exploration of design space: paper instantiates only one configuration (FedAvg→K-means→Local); claims of generality weakened by not comparing alternative level-wise methods (IFCA, FedEM, Ditto at different levels); fixed K=5 justified post-hoc without principled motivation

Convergence rates not explicitly stated: Appendix D provides averaged-stationarity bounds but no explicit rates; lacks quantitative comparison to single-model FedAvg—unclear if the hierarchy provides convergence benefits beyond structure matching

Multi-level construction in foundation model experiments is artificial: assigning exactly one task per client doesn't reflect realistic foundation model usage; unclear how method handles clients with multiple or fractional tasks
